summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon. The offence created in July 2019 was repealed in July 2020: the National Assembly voted 48 in favour, 24 against with 25 abstentions on 23 June 2020, the Senate approved on 29 June 2020, and the president signed on 7 July 2020. The repeal restored the position that had applied since independence.

Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a colonial-era sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence. Article 402 filed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" under "atteintes aux mœurs" without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

The provision was applied while it stood. Two men were arrested under it within months of entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police; the most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2019, and no later instance is documented. Police had also arrested two men in December 2013 accused of conducting a same-sex relationship and released them, before any such offence existed in law.

The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024 under the military government that took power in the August 2023 coup, ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule, rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise same-sex conduct and added privacy protections in Article 18. It does, however, define marriage as a union between two people of opposite sex; that definition took effect on 12 April 2025 and is entrenched as unamendable. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex has no route to recognition of that relationship, and same-sex couples have no legal standing.

Gender identity is treated separately from sexual activity in Gabonese law, and the outcome is thin. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, and no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions that existed concerned same-sex sexual activity, not gender identity.

Police are reported to make occasional use of "breaches of modesty" charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentations and against same-sex couples; sources describe this misuse of neutral provisions as not widespread. State-sponsored harassment of LGBTI people as a group is described as not present, while harassment by individuals is described as common. Neither characterisation is accompanied by a period or a figure in this inventory.

LGBTI groups cannot register as organisations. On the other side of that ledger, Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amended Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011 to treat sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data, which limits how those attributes may be processed and disclosed by holders of personal data.

The age of consent was historically unequal, set at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts. The 2020 reform set the age of sexual majority at 15 for girls and 18 for boys, regardless of partner.

Sources describe religious and ritualistic conversion practices targeting LGBTI people as practised, and describe societal stigmatization of LGBTQIA+ people; neither claim carries a date, a count or a documented case in this inventory. Same-sex relations have generally been legal in Gabon apart from the period between July 2019 and June 2020.
tangentialFactors:
The political background to the current legal position is a rupture rather than a gradual shift. A military coup in August 2023 ended 56 years of rule by the Bongo family, and the constitution approved on 16 November 2024 passed with more than 90 per cent yes on roughly 55 per cent turnout. That process, not a court or a legislature, is what fixed both the privacy provision and the opposite-sex marriage definition now in force.

The 2019 criminalisation and its 2020 reversal were both narrow and both contested. Public opinion on the reversal is reported as sharply divided, and civil society pressed unsuccessfully for re-criminalisation during the 2024 constitutional process. A visitor should read the decriminalisation as a live political question rather than a settled consensus.

The documentary base is uneven. The most detailed official human-rights reporting in this inventory, the US State Department country report, covers 2019 only and therefore captures the year in which the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct together with documented societal discrimination, not the post-repeal period. Later material comes from LGBTI press, an advocacy organisation's country overview, a crime-and-law blog and an encyclopaedic summary, which vary in how carefully they date and source their claims.

Raw-count comparisons of LGBTI incidents across jurisdictions are not usable here: this inventory contains no trans-specific violence count for Gabon at all, and no per-capita figure, so no ranking against other countries can be drawn from it.
localsOnly:
Residents have no procedure for legal gender recognition, so identity documents cannot be brought into line with a person's gender by any administrative route described in this inventory. There is also no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in employment, housing, health care or public services.

LGBTI organisations cannot register, which constrains resident advocacy, mutual support and any formal complaint machinery built on organised groups. Individuals relying on Law No. 025/2023 must invoke the data-protection route themselves, since sexual orientation and sexual life are protected as sensitive personal data rather than as grounds of non-discrimination.

Residents in same-sex relationships have no legal recognition, and the marriage definition entrenched in the November 2024 constitution, effective 12 April 2025, is unamendable on that point. The age of sexual majority stands at 15 for girls and 18 for boys under the 2020 reform.

Reported lived conditions include individual harassment described as common and religious or ritualistic conversion practices described as practised, alongside an absence of state-sponsored group harassment. Both descriptions are undated and unquantified in this inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence figure, killing count or rate appears anywhere in this inventory for Gabon, so no comparison with the country's general homicide rate can be made and none is implied. The absence of such a figure is not evidence of absence of harm.

Nothing in the inventory documents border or airport treatment of transgender travellers: no source addresses document-marker flagging, secondary screening triggered by binders, packers or breast forms, anatomy inspection, or outing risk during entry procedures. Whether Gabonese entry and visa rules permit a marker change, and what a passport with a non-matching gender marker would trigger, is unresolved here.

Whether the 2020 repeal has been tested in court, and whether any arrest, prosecution or "breaches of modesty" charge has been brought after 2020, is unresolved: the most recent documented enforcement in this record dates from 2019, and no later instance is documented. That silence does not establish that such action has ceased.

The claims that individual harassment is common, that conversion practices are widespread, and that police misuse of modesty provisions is not widespread are all undated and unquantified in the sources supplied. The official human-rights reporting available here closes in 2019, so no post-repeal governmental assessment of enforcement or discrimination is on record in this inventory.

Access to gender-affirming health care, the availability of hormone therapy, and treatment of trans patients in Gabonese facilities are not sourced at all. Nor is there any source on how the opposite-sex marriage definition would be applied to a person whose legal gender has been changed elsewhere.
